In [[algebraic geometry]], '''Nagata's compactification theorem''', introduced by {{harvs|txt|last=Nagata|year1=1962|year2=1963|authorlink=Masayoshi Nagata}}, implies that every [[abstract variety]] can be embedded in a [[complete variety]], and more generally shows that a [[Glossary of scheme theory#separated|separated]] and [[Finite morphism#Morphisms of finite type|finite type morphism]] to a [[Noetherian scheme]] ''S'' can be factored into an [[Glossary of scheme theory#immersion|open immersion]] followed by a [[proper morphism]]. 

Nagata's original proof used the older terminology of [[Zariski–Riemann space]]s and [[Valuation (algebra)|valuation theory]], which sometimes made it hard to follow.
[[Pierre Deligne|Deligne]] showed, in unpublished notes expounded by [[Brian Conrad|Conrad]], that Nagata's proof can be translated into scheme theory and that the condition that ''S'' is Noetherian can be replaced by the much weaker condition that ''S'' is [[Compact space|quasi-compact]] and quasi-separated. {{harvtxt|Lütkebohmert|1993}} gave another scheme-theoretic proof of Nagata's theorem.

An important application of Nagata's theorem is in defining the analogue in algebraic geometry of [[cohomology with compact support]], or more generally higher [[Direct image with compact support|direct image functors with proper support]]. The idea is that given a compactifiable morphism <math>f: X \to S,</math> one defines <math>R f_!</math> by choosing a factorization <math>f = p \circ j</math> by an open immersion ''j'' and proper morphism ''p'', and then setting

:<math>Rf_! = Rp_* \circ j_{\sharp}</math>,

where <math>j_{\sharp}</math> is the extension by zero functor. One then shows the independence of the definition from the choice of compactification.

In the context of [[Étale sheaf|étale sheaves]], this idea was carried out by Deligne in [[SGA 4]], Exposé XVII. In the context of [[coherent sheaves]], the statements are more delicate since for an open immersion ''j'', the [[Inverse image functor|inverse image]] functor <math>j^*</math> does not usually admit a left adjoint. Nonetheless, <math>j_{\sharp}</math> exists as a [[nlab:pro-left+adjoint|pro-left adjoint]], and Deligne was able to define the functor <math>R f_!</math> as valued in the pro-derived category of coherent sheaves.<ref>{{citation |last=Hartshorne |first=Robin |title=Residues and duality|publisher=Springer|year=1966 |url=https://eudml.org/doc/203789 |language=EN}} cf. Appendix by P. Deligne.</ref>
